lead: A Pelton wheel takes its energy from a jet of water in air. A Francis or Kaplan turbine takes it from water that stays under pressure inside the machine. The runner stays full of water, the pressure falls as the water crosses it, and a draft tube slows the leaving water and recovers that velocity head as pressure. Francis suits medium heads. Kaplan suits low heads with very large discharges. Most hydel stations, from a 6 m weir to a 200 m dam, use one of these two machines.
prereq: You need: 6.2 velocity triangles and Euler's equation, and 6.1 relative velocity.

sections.h3: A reaction turbine keeps the runner full

blocks.text: In a Pelton wheel the whole head becomes kinetic energy in the nozzle, and the buckets work in air at atmospheric pressure. In a reaction turbine the water enters the runner still under pressure and leaves it at a lower pressure, still moving. Pressure and velocity both change across the runner, so the machine reacts to both. The degree of reaction R compares the two.
R = (pressure head drop in the runner) ÷ (total head across the runner)
blocks.where: R is the degree of reaction (no unit); both heads are in metres of water. For a well-designed Francis runner R is about 0.5, so the guide vanes turn half the head into velocity and the runner takes the other half as a pressure drop.

blocks.text: The water path is fixed by the casing and the vanes around the runner.

items: Spiral casing (scroll): its area shrinks as it goes round, so water reaches the stay ring all round the circle at nearly the same speed.
Stay vanes: fixed vanes that guide the water from the spiral casing to the guide vanes with an even, steady flow, and support the top cover and stay ring.
Guide vanes: adjustable vanes that set the direction and the amount of water entering the runner.
Runner: the pressure drop and the work happen here.
Draft tube: slows the leaving water and recovers head; its theory is in 6.6.

blocks.text: The guide vanes are the throttle. Opening them passes more water; closing them cuts the discharge and the power. No spear or nozzle is needed, because the water is already under pressure. This gives smooth governing, but it also ties discharge to load, which is why a reaction turbine is less forgiving at part load than a Pelton wheel.

A Francis runner is a ring of curved vanes held between a top crown and a bottom band. Water enters at the outer edge, moves inward across the vanes, and leaves at the inner edge near the shaft. It enters radially and leaves axially, so the flow is called mixed flow. A large unit may carry a few hundred cubic metres per second under a head of tens of metres.
The work comes from the change in angular momentum. Euler's equation for the runner is:

blocks.where: H_E is the Euler head in m; u₁ and u₂ are the tangential runner speeds at inlet and outlet in m/s; V_w1 and V_w2 are the whirl components of the absolute velocity at inlet and outlet in m/s; g = 9.81 m/s².

blocks.text: A Francis runner is shaped so the water leaves with almost no whirl, V_w2 ≈ 0 at the design point. All the angular momentum is then given up and H_E = u₁V_w1 ÷ g. The guide vane angle α is measured between the absolute velocity and the wheel tangent; the runner blade angle β₁ is measured between the relative velocity and the tangent. They are different angles, set by different things.

At part load the guide vanes close, V_w1 falls, and the outlet whirl is no longer zero, so the Euler head drops faster than the discharge. Francis efficiency stays high, above 90% in large units, only between roughly 70% and 100% of design flow. Below that the flow leaves the blade surfaces, losses climb, and efficiency falls quickly.

sections.h3: Kaplan: a propeller for low heads

blocks.text: A Kaplan turbine is a propeller turbine with adjustable runner blades. Water flows straight along the shaft axis, with no radial component. The head is low, below about 30 m, and the discharge is very large: what a low head cannot give in pressure it must give in volume. The runner carries only a few blades, so it can pass that volume without choking.

The blade speed is u = πDN ÷ 60, where u is the blade speed in m/s, D is the diameter of that blade section in m (D = 2 × radius of the section), and N is the runner speed in rpm. The radius changes from hub to tip, so u grows from root to tip. The blade must therefore be twisted: set steeply near the hub and flatter near the tip, so each section meets the water at its own correct angle. That twist is why a Kaplan blade looks like a ship's propeller.

A Kaplan turbine is double-regulated: the governor moves the guide vanes and the runner blade angle together. As load falls, the blades turn to keep V_w2 near zero, so efficiency stays high down to about 30% of full load. A fixed-blade propeller turbine is efficient only near its design point, which is why the adjustable version is the one used where load changes through the day.

Cavitation risk follows the draft tube. It puts the runner above tailwater at sub-atmospheric pressure, so water can boil at the blade surface. A Kaplan passes the most water, so it has the highest cavitation risk and must be set lowest below tailwater. Specific speed ranges and their units are covered in 6.7.

examples.question: A Francis turbine runner has a tangential speed at inlet u₁ = 20 m/s and an inlet whirl component V_w1 = 18 m/s. At outlet the whirl component is zero. The net head at the runner inlet, after casing, stay vane and guide vane losses are removed, is 45 m. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find (a) the Euler head and (b) the hydraulic efficiency.
steps: Write Euler's equation for the runner: H_E = (u₁V_w1 − u₂V_w2) ÷ g.
Outlet whirl is zero, so V_w2 = 0 and the second term u₂V_w2 vanishes whatever u₂ is.
H_E = 360 ÷ 9.81 = 36.70 m. This is the head the runner actually converts.
Hydraulic efficiency is the Euler head divided by the net head at the runner inlet: η_h = H_E ÷ H_net = 36.70 ÷ 45.

η_h = 0.815, that is 81.5%. The other 18.5% is friction and eddy loss inside the runner, plus the exit kinetic energy that the draft tube does not recover. The draft tube sits after the runner, so its loss lowers the overall efficiency, not the head at the runner inlet.
examples.answer: Euler head H_E = 36.7 m and hydraulic efficiency η_h = 81.5%.
examples.check:
u1 = 20.0      # m/s, inlet blade speed
Vw1 = 18.0     # m/s, inlet whirl
u2 = 0.0
Vw2 = 0.0      # m/s, no whirl at outlet
g = 9.81       # m/s**2
H_net = 45.0   # m, net head at runner

H_E = (u1 * Vw1 - u2 * Vw2) / g   # Euler head, m
eta_h = H_E / H_net               # hydraulic efficiency

print(round(H_E, 1))
print(round(eta_h * 100, 1))

traps: Using the guide vane angle α in place of the runner blade angle β₁. α lies between the absolute velocity and the tangent; β₁ lies between the relative velocity and the tangent.

Putting the gross head into the hydraulic efficiency. Use the net head at the runner inlet, after casing, stay vane and guide vane losses. An efficiency above 100% means the head used was too small — for example the head measured after the runner, or a head with the same losses subtracted twice.
Treating V_w2 = 0 as always true. It holds at the design point only; at part load the leaving whirl comes back and the Euler head falls.
Saying a Kaplan is governed by the guide vanes alone. It is double-regulated: the runner blade angle moves with the vane opening.
Swapping the runners: Francis is mixed flow, radial in and axial out; Kaplan is axial throughout, with twisted adjustable blades.

quiz.q: Name, in order, the five parts the water passes through in a Francis turbine, from the penstock to the tailrace.
quiz.a: Spiral casing, stay vanes, guide vanes, runner, draft tube.

quiz.q: Why is a reaction turbine governed by guide vanes instead of a spear and nozzle?
quiz.a: The water is already under pressure when it reaches the runner, so there is no free jet to deflect. Turning the guide vanes changes both the direction and the quantity of water entering the runner, which changes the power directly. A spear only works on a free jet in air, as in a Pelton wheel.

quiz.q: A Francis runner has u₁ = 15 m/s, V_w1 = 14 m/s, u₂ = 9 m/s and V_w2 = 2 m/s. The net head at the runner is 30 m. Find the Euler head and the hydraulic efficiency. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
A Francis turbine and a double-regulated Kaplan both run at 40% of design flow. Which keeps the higher efficiency, and why?
quiz.a: The Kaplan. Its runner blades turn as the guide vanes close, so each blade keeps meeting the reduced flow at a small incidence and the outlet whirl stays near zero. The Francis blades are fixed, so at 40% flow the inlet angle no longer matches β₁, the outlet whirl becomes non-zero, and separation losses rise on both sides of the vane.

quiz.q: Why must a Kaplan runner blade be twisted from hub to tip, while a Pelton bucket is not?
quiz.a: Blade speed is u = πDN ÷ 60, and D changes from hub to tip on a Kaplan, so u and the direction of the relative velocity change along the blade. Each section needs its own blade angle. Every Pelton bucket runs at one radius with one u, so one bucket shape fits.

quiz.q: A Kaplan runner of diameter 4 m runs at 150 rpm. Find the blade speed at the tip.

beyond: Not for the exam. A Francis runner can be run backwards as a pump, and that reversible machine is the heart of pumped storage, where water is lifted at night and released at peak; India's pumped storage plans rest on it. Blade shapes today are refined with CFD rather than hand-drawn velocity triangles, and small hydro in hilly districts leans on low-head Kaplan and semi-Kaplan units. Search for pump-turbine, double-regulated Kaplan and model testing of Francis runners to go further.
